lessons.title: When DCF and Multiples Disagree: Reconciling Your Valuations

children.text: Work through a company properly and you will end up with more than one answer. A DCF says one thing, the peer multiple says another, and the market price says a third. Beginners average them. Professionals do something more useful: they treat the disagreement as information and work out exactly which assumption creates it.

body.text: Never average your methods. Translate each into the other's language: what multiple does my DCF imply, and what growth and returns does the peer multiple imply? The explanation for the gap is worth more than either number.

children.text: Step 1: Rule Out Mechanical Errors First
Before concluding that the market disagrees with you, make sure you have not simply made a mistake. Most large gaps between a DCF and a multiple come from one of these.

body.caption: Check these before interpreting any gap

cells: Enterprise or equity?
Comparing a DCF equity value with an EV-based multiple, or forgetting to subtract net debt
Share count
Basic shares in one method, fully diluted in the other
Earnings basis
Multiple built on reported EPS that includes one-off gains, while the DCF uses clean operating cash flows
Consolidated or standalone
DCF on consolidated cash flows, peer multiples on standalone earnings
Leases
Reported EBITDA under Ind AS 116 without adding lease liabilities to enterprise value
Cycle position
A DCF built on mid-cycle margins, compared with a peer multiple calculated on peak earnings
Bridge items
Contingent liabilities, minority interests or surplus assets included in one method and not the other

children.text: Step 2: Translate the DCF Into Multiples

Take Kaveri Ridge Cement, the company built up through Chapters 2, 3 and 4. Its DCF gave an enterprise value of ₹8,054 crore and a value of ₹248.6 per share. It earns EBITDA of ₹1,300 crore and net profit of ₹660 crore, which on 25.6 crore diluted shares is EPS of ₹25.8. Net debt is ₹1,500 crore and the shares trade at ₹300.

body.caption: The same company expressed three ways

cells: DCF
Market price
Cement peer median

stats.label: Gap to explain
stats.context: Between the DCF and the EV/EBITDA answer

body.text: Once translated, the disagreement becomes precise. The DCF says Kaveri Ridge is worth 6.20 times EBITDA; its peers trade at 7.5 times. That is now a researchable question: is Kaveri Ridge genuinely worth less per rupee of EBITDA than its peers, or is one of my DCF assumptions too harsh?

children.text: Why the P/E answer is the highest, and the least reliable

Applying the peer P/E of 14× gives ₹360.9, the most generous of the three answers. Chapter 4 explained why to distrust it here: Kaveri Ridge carries ₹1,500 crore of net debt, and P/E comparisons across companies with different leverage are unreliable. Cement is also cyclical, so the "E" depends on where realisations sit in the cycle. For this business, EV/EBITDA on mid-cycle EBITDA is the more trustworthy cross-check, and the DCF is the primary method.
Step 3: Find the Source of the Disagreement

body.caption: Diagnosing a gap between a DCF and a peer multiple

cells: DCF well below peer multiples
Your growth, margin or terminal assumptions are more conservative than the market's
Reverse DCF: what growth does the peer multiple imply?
DCF well above peer multiples
Optimistic forecasts, or the peer group is depressed for a real reason
Compare your forecast with the company's own history and peer performance
DCF and multiples agree, both above market price
Possible genuine mispricing, or a risk you have not captured
Contingent liabilities, governance, pledged shares, liquidity
Peer P/E and peer EV/EBITDA disagree with each other
Leverage or depreciation differences within the peer set
Trust EV/EBITDA where debt levels differ; check capex intensity
Both methods swing wildly year to year
The business is cyclical and earnings are not normalised
Rebuild on mid-cycle earnings, as in Chapter 5
Multiples look cheap, DCF looks expensive
Peak earnings inflating the denominator of the multiple
Compare current margin with the ten-year average

children.text: For Kaveri Ridge, the ₹74 gap has identifiable sources. Its DCF deducts half of a disputed mining royalty demand, a probability-weighted cost that peer multiples do not reflect at all. Its WACC of 11.5% reflects its own leverage, while the peer median blends companies with less debt. And the DCF assumes a fade to 5% perpetual growth, where the peer multiple implicitly assumes whatever the market currently expects for the sector. None of these is a mistake. Together they explain why one number is lower.

columns.label: Lead with the DCF when
points: Cash flows are predictable: FMCG, IT services, utilities
The peer set is poor, tiny or distorted
The whole sector may be mispriced
The company is loss-making or early-stage, where multiples do not exist
Capital structure or accounting differs sharply from peers

columns.label: Lead with multiples when
points: Forecasting is genuinely unreliable: deep cyclicals, commodity producers
There are many close, comparable listed peers
You are valuing a lender, where P/B against ROE is the natural anchor
The valuation is for a transaction priced on market terms
You need a quick sanity check on a DCF you have just built

body.label: The rule that prevents most mistakes
body.value: Weight by reliability, never by convenience
body.context: Ask which method's key input you trust more: your ten-year forecast, or the market's pricing of the peer group. Then say so explicitly in your notes, with your reason.

children.text: The output of reconciliation is not a single reconciled number. It is a range, with the market price marked on it, and a sentence explaining the spread.

body.title: Kaveri Ridge Cement: value per share by method (₹)

children.text: Read as a whole, the picture is clear. Kaveri Ridge is worth roughly ₹203 to ₹361 depending on method and assumptions, with the methods you should trust most for a leveraged cyclical, the DCF and EV/EBITDA, clustering between ₹203 and ₹322. The market price of ₹300 sits inside that range, towards the upper half. That is a far more honest conclusion than "the stock is worth ₹310.6", which is what averaging the three methods would produce.

body.text: Averaging methods hides the disagreement that was the most valuable output of your work. Worse, it lets a method you do not trust pull the answer. If you must produce a single number for a report, use the method you judge most reliable, state it plainly, and show the others as a range around it.

body.title: Translate a DCF into a multiple
body.prompt: Your DCF gives an enterprise value of ₹9,600 crore for a company with EBITDA of ₹1,200 crore. What EV/EBITDA multiple does your DCF imply?
body.explanation: ₹9,600 crore ÷ ₹1,200 crore = 8.0×. Compare this with the peer median. If peers trade at 11× and your DCF implies 8×, your assumptions are more conservative than the market's, and you should be able to say exactly which one.

body.title: Translate a multiple into a price
body.prompt: A company has EBITDA of ₹900 crore, net debt of ₹2,000 crore and 40 crore shares. Its peer median EV/EBITDA is 8×. What value per share does the peer multiple imply, in ₹?
body.explanation: EV = 8 × ₹900 crore = ₹7,200 crore. Equity = ₹7,200 - ₹2,000 = ₹5,200 crore. Per share = ₹5,200 ÷ 40 = ₹130. Now compare it with your DCF and explain any gap.

body.title: Which method leads?
body.question: You are valuing an aluminium producer during a period of unusually high metal prices. Your DCF, built on mid-cycle realisations, gives a value 30% below the price implied by the peer median P/E. Which conclusion is best supported?
options: The DCF is wrong because the market disagrees with it
Average the two methods and use the midpoint
The peer P/E is being calculated on peak earnings, so the DCF on mid-cycle assumptions deserves more weight; check the peers' margins against their long-run averages
Use the peer P/E because it reflects real transactions
body.explanation: During a commodity upcycle, trailing P/Es across the whole peer group are calculated on peak profits, so they look low and imply high prices. A DCF on normalised, mid-cycle assumptions is the more reliable anchor, as Chapter 5 showed. The correct next step is to verify that peer earnings really are at a peak.

body.title: The reconciliation habit
body.textWithBlank: To reconcile a DCF with peer multiples, ___ each method into the other's language before deciding which to trust.
body.explanation: Convert your DCF into an implied P/E and EV/EBITDA, and convert the peer multiple into an implied growth rate through a reverse DCF. The gap then becomes a specific, answerable question.

body.title: The analyst who averaged
body.scenario: Vishal, a junior analyst at a Mumbai brokerage, values a listed pharma company three ways: a DCF gives ₹1,150 per share; the peer median P/E of 32× on FY27 estimated EPS gives ₹1,680; and an EV/EBITDA comparison gives ₹1,320. He averages the three to reach ₹1,383 and sets that as his target price, against a market price of ₹1,400. The company earns 60% of revenue from the US generics market, where price erosion has been severe, while the peer group is weighted towards domestic branded formulations. His DCF assumes 6% revenue growth; the peer set is growing at 12%.
body.prompt: What is wrong with Vishal's approach, and what should he do instead?
body.modelAnswer:
1. Averaging hides the problem. Three methods disagreeing by ₹530 per share is the finding. Averaging them produces a number no method supports and conceals the reason for the spread.
2. The peer set is wrong. As Chapter 4 showed, US generics exporters and domestic branded formulation companies have different growth, margins and returns. Applying a peer median built mostly from branded companies to a generics exporter guarantees an inflated answer.
3. The growth assumptions contradict each other. His DCF assumes 6% growth while the peer multiple embeds 12%. Both cannot be right for the same company. That single inconsistency explains most of the gap.
4. What he should do: rebuild the peer set using US-focused generics exporters only, and recompute the median P/E and EV/EBITDA. Translate his DCF into implied multiples and compare like with like. Run a reverse DCF on the ₹1,400 market price to see what growth and margins it requires, and test that against price erosion trends in the US market.
5. How to present it: lead with the DCF, since the peer set is weak and the business faces a specific structural headwind; show the multiple-based values as a range around it; and state in one sentence why the peer-based numbers are higher.

body.title: Reconciliation routine
steps: Confirm both methods use the same share count, the same consolidation basis and the same treatment of leases and one-offs.
Convert your DCF value into an implied P/E, EV/EBITDA and P/B.
Convert the peer median multiple into a value per share.
Run a reverse DCF on the market price to see the growth and margins it implies.
Write one sentence naming the assumption that explains most of the gap.
Decide which method leads, based on the business type and the quality of the peer set.
Present a range with the market price marked, not an average.

points: Disagreement between methods is information, not a problem to be averaged away.
Rule out mechanical errors first: enterprise versus equity, share counts, one-off earnings, lease treatment and consolidation basis.
Translate the DCF into implied multiples and the peer multiple into a value per share, so the gap becomes a specific question.
Lead with the DCF for predictable businesses, poor peer sets or possible sector-wide mispricing; lead with multiples for deep cyclicals, close peers and transactions.
For leveraged or cyclical companies, trust EV/EBITDA over P/E, and normalise earnings before either.
Present a range with the market price marked on it, and name the assumption that drives the spread.

body.text: This lesson is for education only and is not investment advice. Kaveri Ridge Cement Ltd, the pharma company described and the individuals named are fictional, and all figures are illustrative. Consult a SEBI-registered investment adviser before making investment decisions.
